summary: Supply-chain traceability is a growing security concern. This document defines an architecture for transparency of signed statements from a single issuer using Verifiable Data Structures.

plainLanguage.summary: A supply chain record should be tamper-proof. This design makes a public logbook so signed statements about products cannot quietly change.

questions: how does scitt relate to certificate transparency
subtitle: A common notary-style architecture that makes signed statements about supply chain artifacts publicly auditable.

tldr.problem: Supply chain attacks hit many stages of building and shipping software, and the statements about a product (SBOMs, test results, approvals) are varied and easy to hide or quietly change.
tldr.mechanism: Issuers sign statements as COSE_Sign1 messages. A Transparency Service checks them against a Registration Policy, adds them to an append-only Verifiable Data Structure and returns a signed Receipt. A statement with a Receipt attached is a Transparent Statement.
tldr.outcome: Relying Parties can check who made a statement and that it was recorded, and Auditors can replay the log. Transparency does not stop dishonest Issuers but holds them accountable.

today: RFC 9943 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2026. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the metadata. It builds on RFC 9942 for the Receipt format.

sections.title: The Supply Chain Problem
sections.content:
RFC 9943 defines the Supply Chain Integrity, Transparency, and Trust (SCITT) architecture. Its stated goal is to improve auditability and accountability for single-issuer signed statements about supply chain commodities, called artifacts.

The RFC points out that an attack can hit one or more life-cycle stages: dependencies, code, commit, build, test, package, release and deploy. Statements about a product are varied: commit signatures, SBOMs, security test results, release approvals, deployment records and patch logs. Rather than describe every kind, SCITT focuses on authenticity, visibility and scalable access, and on making statement makers accountable so they cannot "hide or shred the evidence" later.

For examples the RFC limits itself to the software supply chain: a security analysis of a product, a component promoted by several providers, and an integrator assembling software for a vehicle. It says the design applies to other supply chains too.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a toy passes through many hands before reaching you. If anyone can secretly change the notes about it, you cannot trust the toy. SCITT keeps honest, signed notes that nobody can hide.

sections.title: The Cast of Roles
sections.content:
The terminology section fixes a small vocabulary. An Issuer is an organization, device or user that makes Statements about an Artifact. The Issuer wraps a Statement in an Envelope (COSE headers) and signs it, producing a Signed Statement.

A Transparency Service (TS) maintains and extends a Verifiable Data Structure (VDS) and endorses its state. Registration is submitting a Signed Statement, applying the TS Registration Policy, adding it to the VDS and producing a Receipt. A Signed Statement plus a Receipt is a Transparent Statement.

Relying Parties consume Transparent Statements. An Auditor is a specialized Relying Party that checks the correctness and consistency of everything a TS has issued.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone writes a note and signs it (the Issuer). A librarian (the Transparency Service) files it in a book that can only grow and hands back a stamped slip. Anyone can later read the book and check the slips.

sections.title: What Transparency Means
sections.content:
Transparency here is built from an append-only log and Receipts. A Receipt is a signature over one or more proofs that a Signed Statement is in the VDS, and it is universally verifiable without online access to the TS. Anyone with access to the TS can verify its consistency and list the Transparent Statements registered by each Issuer.

The RFC is careful about the limits: transparency does not prevent dishonest or compromised Issuers, but it holds them accountable. Reputable Issuers have a reason to review statements before signing, and TSs have a reason to protect their VDS, because any inconsistency can be pinpointed by an Auditor.

The RFC calls SCITT a generalization of Certificate Transparency (RFC 9162): CAs are Issuers, certificates are Signed Statements, CT logs are TSs and Signed Certificate Timestamps are Transparent Statements.
sections.plainLanguage: The logbook cannot stop someone from writing a fib. But the fib stays in the book with their signature on it, so they cannot pretend they never said it.

sections.title: The Transparency Service
sections.content:
A TS MUST produce COSE Receipts (RFC 9942). Its VDS must provide three properties: append-only (statements cannot be modified, deleted or reordered), non-equivocation (no fork, so everyone sees the same ordered collection) and replayability (enough information for authorized actors to check each statement was registered correctly).

Before registering, a TS applies Registration Policies. It MUST verify the COSE signature, bind the Issuer identity to the statement through an identifier in the protected header, and keep a list of trust anchors. For X.509 it must build a full certification path to a registered root. Policies and trust anchors themselves MUST be made transparent by registering them as Signed Statements, and the policy applied is the one most recently committed to the VDS.

Because those checks depend on registered policy, a TS MUST support at least one bootstrapping mechanism: a preconfigured policy and trust anchors, acceptance of a first Signed Statement whose payload is a valid policy, or an out-of-band authenticated management interface. The RFC prefers registration-based bootstrapping, since preconfigured values that cannot be updated suit long-lived services poorly.
sections.plainLanguage: The librarian has a rulebook that is itself kept in the public book. Before filing a note, the librarian checks the signature and the rules, so nobody can change the rules in secret.

sections.title: Signed and Transparent Statements
sections.content:
A Signed Statement is a COSE_Sign1 message. The protected header MUST include the CWT Claims parameter (label 15) with an Issuer (iss, label 1) and a Subject (sub, label 2). If the header carries x5t or x5chain, the iss value MUST be a URI string of 1 to 8192 characters; otherwise a kid is required. The payload type is the Issuer's choice, for example CoSWID, CycloneDX, in-toto, SPDX or SLSA.

For payloads that are large or sensitive, the statement can be made over the hash of the payload, and the payload can be detached (nil).

To register, a Client authenticates (how is out of scope), the TS verifies the signature and required headers, applies the Registration Policy, registers the statement and returns a Receipt. The Receipt may be asynchronous, but the TS MUST register a statement before releasing its Receipt and MUST be able to provide a Receipt for all registered statements. The unprotected header must be an empty map before inclusion in the log.

Adding the Receipt to the unprotected header (label 394, an array of Receipts) yields a Transparent Statement. One statement may be registered in several TSs, collecting several Receipts. An Issuer that learns an artifact's quality has changed SHOULD register a new Signed Statement with the same iss and sub.
sections.plainLanguage: A signed note has a sender name and a topic name on the front. When the librarian stamps it, the stamp is clipped on without changing the note. You can collect stamps from several libraries.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
SCITT claims three guarantees: statements are identifiable and authenticable, their provenance and history can be independently and consistently audited, and Issuers can efficiently prove their statement is logged.

Limits are stated plainly. Registering a statement only proves an Issuer produced it, not that it is true. Unless a Registration Policy says so, ordering in the VDS need not match the order of issuance. Issuers can skip registration or submit selectively, so Relying Parties should not accept Signed Statements for which they cannot find Receipts from a TS they trust. Issuers and TSs MUST protect private keys, avoid using a key for more than one purpose and rotate keys at an appropriate cryptoperiod.

No single central TS is required; Relying Parties choose which TSs and Issuers to trust. Relying Parties and Auditors need not be trusted, and cannot "frame" an Issuer or TS who keeps control of their keys. On privacy, the TS is trusted with the confidentiality of submitted statements, and metadata analysis across the TS and adjacent services could reveal the order in which artifacts were built, signed and uploaded.
sections.plainLanguage: The logbook proves who said what, not that they told the truth. You decide which signers and which librarians you trust, and keep your keys safe.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA has registered two media types, application/scitt-statement+cose (file extension .scitt) and application/scitt-receipt+cose (file extension .receipt). Both describe binary CBOR data items.

IANA also registered CoAP Content-Format IDs 277 for the statement type and 278 for the receipt type.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of file gets an official name tag so computers know what they are looking at.

layers.detail: Signed proofs from one or more TSs

layers.detail: CWT Claims with iss and sub, plus alg, content type and key identifiers

layers.detail: Opaque to the TS; may be detached
